1317.title: sleep
1317.hook: deep sleep leaves nothing to tell at breakfast; the Brihadaranyaka describes it anyway, with a falcon
1317.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers study deep, dreamless sleep, sushupti, beside waking and dreaming, and read Yajnavalkya's falcon as a picture of the self at rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep and the dream: the dreamer self-lit, making chariots and rivers where there are none.

Deep sleep is the one part of the night with nothing to report. No dream to tell over breakfast. Just a gap, and then the alarm. A gap seems an odd thing to teach. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tries anyway. Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, has walked through waking and through dreams. Now he goes one step further down, and to describe it, he reaches for a bird. Today, the sleep with no dreams in it.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `A GAP, THEN THE ALARM.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the bird, paraphrased. A falcon, or an eagle, has been flying in the open sky. It's tired, so it folds its wings and drops to its nest. In the same way, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, he wants nothing at all and sees no dream. Then Yajnavalkya says something stranger. There, a father is not a father, a mother is not a mother. The worlds are not worlds, the gods not gods, the Vedas not Vedas. A thief is not a thief. He is untouched by good and untouched by evil, the text says, for he has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart. Three things. First, the folded wings. The falcon isn't defeated. It flew all day; folding the wings is just the other half of flying. Second, the roles. Every name a person carries by day, parent, worker, friend, the one with a reputation, even the one with a past, is set down in deep sleep. Not erased. Set down. In the morning they're picked back up. Third, the sorrows of the heart. The text doesn't say grief is cured. It says only that, in that state, the sleeper has crossed over it: a nightly crossing, made without effort. And for honesty: Yajnavalkya isn't saying the goal of life is to sleep well. Deep sleep, for him, is a clue, a nightly taste of being without wanting. The Mandukya Upanishad lines up waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and points past all of them.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER` · `THE SORROWS OF THE HEART, CROSSED` · `A CLUE, NOT THE GOAL`

segments.voice: Name, silently, one role you carried today, parent, worker, friend, student, the one who has to answer, and with the next breath out set it down beside you, not thrown away, just put down. Then the next, and when there are no more names, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
Sleep. In deep sleep, the Brihadaranyaka says, a person wants nothing, sees no dream, and has crossed the sorrows of the heart, like a falcon folding its wings. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Every name is set down for the night, and picked up again in the morning. See you tomorrow.

1318.title: sleep
1318.hook: "I slept well": a commentator on the Yoga Sutras asks how anyone could know that
1318.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn sleep as one of the five vrittis, the movements of the mind, usually alongside Vyasa's commentary on the sutras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep with no dreams: the falcon folding its wings, every daytime name set down.

"I slept well." It gets said over coffee, in a hallway, in a text to someone who asked. Hardly a controversial sentence. But stop on it for a second. Who was there to notice? If the mind was simply gone all night, switched off like a lamp, how does it come back with a report? Somebody asked exactly that, a long time ago, in a commentary on the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. Today, sleep as something the mind is doing.
screen: `I SLEPT WELL.` → `WHO WAS THERE TO NOTICE?` → `A COMMENTATOR ASKS.`

segments.voice: Start with the sutra. Early in the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali lists the movements of the mind, the vrittis, the turnings that yoga learns to quiet. He names five: right knowing, error, imagination, sleep and memory. Sleep is on the list, not as the mind's absence, but as one of its movements. He defines it in one compact line, paraphrased: sleep is the turning of the mind that rests on absence, on the experience of nothing. Then the commentary traditionally credited to Vyasa adds the morning. Paraphrased: on waking, a person says, I slept well, my mind is clear. Or: I slept badly, my mind is heavy and dull. That memory, the commentary argues, shows that sleep was experienced. You can't remember what never happened to you. This shifts a few things. First, what sleep is: not a hole in the day, but a state with its own quality, light or heavy, clear or dull, which the mind brings back into the morning. Second, why sleep belongs in a book about practice. If it's a movement of the mind, it's part of the mind's weather, and the night's weather shapes the day's. Third, the Yoga Sutras go further. Later in the first chapter, one way offered for steadying the mind is to rest it on what is known from dream and from sleep. The night, again, becomes material for practice. And as with every day in this lens: the Yoga Sutras describe the mind; they don't diagnose sleep. If nights are often heavy and mornings dull for a long stretch, that's a conversation for a doctor.
screen: `FIVE TURNINGS OF THE MIND` · `SLEEP RESTS ON ABSENCE` · `I SLEPT WELL: A MEMORY` · `THE NIGHT AS MATERIAL FOR PRACTICE`

segments.voice: Go back to last night's sleep, not the hours but the quality, light or heavy, clear or tangled, and find one honest word for it. Then notice that the mind just remembered a night it was supposedly absent for, and rest in that for a few breaths. If you pray, give thanks for whatever rest there was.
Sleep. In the Yoga Sutras, one of the mind's five turnings, resting on absence, and remembered in the morning as light or heavy. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Even a night you can't recall leaves a morning report. I'll be here tomorrow.

1319.title: sleep
1319.hook: drums, conches and elephants: Lanka tries to wake a sleeping giant, and he wakes up honest
1319.howItsDone: Kumbhakarna's waking is told in Ramayana retellings and Ramlila performances, and Hindu teachers draw on Gita 14 to explain tamas, the quality of heaviness, as one of the three gunas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yoga Sutras: sleep as a movement of the mind, remembered in the morning as light or heavy.

Drums are pounding. Conches are blowing. People are shouting into a giant's ears, and elephants are being led over his sleeping body. Next to him, food is heaped up for the moment his eyes open. It's Lanka, in Valmiki's Ramayana, and the city is under siege. Ravana needs his brother Kumbhakarna, and Kumbhakarna is asleep. Getting him up takes a crowd. Today, the sleep that isn't rest, and what a giant says when he finally wakes.
screen: `DRUMS, CONCHES, ELEPHANTS.` → `A CITY UNDER SIEGE.` → `THE GIANT IS ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: Kumbhakarna is Ravana's brother, a giant the story knows for his long sleeps. Tradition tells that his sleep came from a boon that went wrong, a wish that came out as sleep. Now the war has started without him. When he finally wakes, hungry and enormous, he eats, and he's brought to his brother. Then the surprise. Ravana tells him what has happened: the taking of Sita, the army at the walls. And Kumbhakarna, the sleepy one, tells the king the truth to his face. Paraphrased: you did this without listening to counsel; you acted first and thought after. Then, out of loyalty, he goes out to fight for his brother anyway, and he falls. Three ways in. First, the Gita names this kind of sleep. Its fourteenth chapter describes tamas, the quality of darkness and heaviness, and says it binds a person through heedlessness, laziness and sleep. Not sleep as rest, which the texts honor, but sleep as staying under, as not wanting to wake. Second, the story is fairer than a cartoon. The giant who slept through the war's beginning is the one who, once awake, speaks plainly to the king. Waking up can be an honest moment. Third, the ordinary version: a hard email, a bill, a conversation put off for months. There's a kind of Kumbhakarna sleep that has nothing to do with a bed. And one careful note: tiredness that won't lift is a matter for a doctor, never a mark of bad character. The Gita's tamas names a pull to stay under, not a diagnosis of anyone.
screen: `KUMBHAKARNA, KNOWN FOR HIS SLEEP` · `YOU ACTED WITHOUT COUNSEL` · `TAMAS BINDS THROUGH SLEEP` · `THE SLEEP THAT ISN'T ABOUT A BED`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that you've been sleeping through, something put off or unanswered, and let it sit in front of you while you breathe, without solving it or scolding yourself. Then find the smallest first step, one sentence or one look, and hold it lightly. If you pray, ask for help with it.
Sleep. In the Gita, one of the ways tamas binds; in the Ramayana, Kumbhakarna's long sleep, and the honest words he speaks when he wakes. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Waking up, even late, can be an honest moment. Go gently.

1320.title: sleep
1320.hook: a sage wakes two sleeping princes by a river, and his words become a temple's dawn song
1320.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1320.howItsDone: The Venkatesa Suprabhatam is sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in homes in the morning, and some temples close the day with a rite that lays the deity to rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep that isn't rest: Kumbhakarna, woken by drums and elephants, and the honest words he spoke once awake.

Before sunrise, by a river, two young princes are asleep on the ground. The sage leading them, Vishvamitra, leans over and speaks. Paraphrased: Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the eastern dawn is breaking. Rise, tiger among men; the day's rites are waiting. It's a small moment early in Valmiki's Ramayana, a teacher waking his students. But those words didn't stay by the river. They became the opening of a hymn sung before dawn to wake the deity. Today, the last of the sleep days: the temple's night and morning.
screen: `TWO PRINCES ASLEEP BY A RIVER.` → `RAMA, THE DAWN IS BREAKING.` → `A HYMN TO WAKE GOD.`

segments.voice: The hymn is the Venkatesa Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala. Suprabhatam means a good dawn. It opens with Vishvamitra's verse, then turns to the Lord of the hill and asks him, verse after verse, to wake. At the other end of the day, some temples have a bedtime rite. The deity is laid to rest, the lamps are lowered, a last song is sung, and the doors are shut until morning. A few things to see. First, tradition speaks of these rites as care, not as a claim that God gets tired: the way a beloved member of the household is served. A day with God in it begins with a gentle waking and ends with a gentle night. Second, the waking is spoken. Vishvamitra doesn't shake the princes. He tells them the dawn is here and the day has work in it. A good waking names what's waiting. Third, the two ends of the day frame everything between. Look back over the sleep days. Charaka counted sleep among the three supports of life. Uddalaka's bird settled at its tether, the mind at rest in the breath. Yajnavalkya's dreamer was self-lit, making chariots and rivers. His falcon folded its wings, and every daytime name was set down. The Yoga Sutras read the morning report: I slept well. Kumbhakarna woke up honest. And here, the night and the dawn held as worship. Tomorrow, the breath, quietly running under all of it.
screen: `SUPRABHATAM: A GOOD DAWN` · `A BEDTIME RITE IN THE TEMPLE` · `CARE, NOT A CLAIM OF TIREDNESS` · `THE TWO ENDS FRAME THE DAY`

segments.voice: Picture the last moment before sleep tonight, gently, a lamp lowered, a door shut, and then the first moment of tomorrow: not shaken awake, but spoken to, with one kind sentence. Rest between the two, breathing. If you pray, offer the night and the morning both.
Sleep. A support of life, a homecoming, a self-lit dream, a falcon's nest, a movement of the mind, a giant's waking, and a temple's night and dawn. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. A gentle night, and a dawn that's spoken to. Rest well, and see you at dawn.

1321.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1321.hook: breath gets asked to carry cures, hacks and hidden energies; this stretch checks every claim against the page
1321.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1321.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1321.howItsDone: Some yoga teachers who follow Patanjali have students watch the breath before regulating it, and adapt or skip breath-holding for students with health conditions.

segments.voice: Last week closed on sleep: a temple's bedtime and its dawn song, and Rama woken with words.

A sticky note on a bathroom mirror says: just breathe. Fair enough. But breath gets asked to carry a lot more these days. One trick to fix your sleep. One pattern to melt stress away. An ancient secret energy, now in an app. Some of it may help. Some is said with more confidence than the evidence has earned. These last days of the Ayurveda lens come back to the breath, with a promise in the title. Today, the breath again, every claim checked.
screen: `JUST BREATHE.` → `A TRICK, A PATTERN, A SECRET.` → `EVERY CLAIM CHECKED.`

segments.voice: First, the rule for these days. Every claim about breath gets one of three labels. The text says: a line you can find on the page, with a reference. Tradition says: what teachers and families pass down, honored, but not the same as the page. A doctor decides: anything about illness, cure or treatment. This path won't promise a cure. Now one claim, checked. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, in the second chapter, describe the breath in practice. Paraphrased: its movement out, its movement in, and its pause, when watched by place, by time and by number, becomes long and fine. The Sanskrit for that last pair is dirgha sukshma, long and subtle. What kind of claim is that? Not a promise about blood pressure or sleep. It describes what happens to breath under attention, and it hands over the method: notice where the breath is felt, how long it lasts, how many there are. Anyone can check it, gently, by watching. Label: the text says, and the watching is yours. Now what the sutra doesn't say. It doesn't say breathe in a special pattern to heal. It offers no number of seconds. Those come from other texts and other teachers, and when they come up, they'll get their own labels. One plain safety line, because breath work isn't neutral. Anyone with a heart or lung condition, anyone pregnant, anyone who gets dizzy or anxious with breath exercises, keeps to easy natural breathing and asks a doctor before any holding of the breath. Today's practice holds nothing. It only watches.
screen: `THREE LABELS FOR EVERY CLAIM` · `WATCHED BY PLACE, TIME AND NUMBER` · `DIRGHA SUKSHMA: LONG AND FINE` · `WHAT THE SUTRA DOESN'T SAY`

segments.voice: Let the breath do whatever it's doing, and check it by place, where it's felt most, then by time, whether the in-breath runs longer than the out-breath, then by number, counting a few breaths from one to five, without changing anything. If it grows longer and finer on its own, notice that; if it doesn't, that's an honest result too. If you pray, let the breath be your prayer.
The breath again. In the Yoga Sutras, breath watched by place, time and number becomes long and fine: a claim you can check by watching. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. The text says, tradition says, a doctor decides. That's today, done.

1322.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1322.hook: the senses quarrel over who holds the body up, and breath settles it by getting up to leave
1322.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1322.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1322.howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Prashna Upanishad's quarrel of the senses as a teaching about what keeps a being alive, and some Hindus sit with the breath as a daily practice of attention.

segments.voice: Last time, the breath again, with a promise attached: every claim checked. Today the checking begins.

An argument breaks out inside a body. Speech says it holds the body up. So does the mind. So do the eye and the ear. Each one is sure it's the pillar. Then breath, the quiet one, says nothing much. It just starts to leave. And the moment it lifts, every other power is dragged up with it, whether it likes it or not. This story sits in the second question of the Prashna Upanishad, a text built as six students asking a teacher six questions. Today: what it means by breath, and one popular claim, checked against the page.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT INSIDE A BODY.` → `BREATH STARTS TO LEAVE.` → `ONE CLAIM, CHECKED AGAINST THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, in paraphrase. A student asks the teacher Pippalada which powers hold a being together, and which of them is greatest. The teacher tells the quarrel. The elements and the senses each claim the body. Breath warns them not to be fooled: it alone, dividing itself, keeps the body standing. They don't believe it. So breath rises to go, and they all rise with it. It settles, and they all settle, like bees following their king bee out of the hive and back again. Then the senses sing to breath, and the hymn makes it very large. Breath burns as fire, shines as the sun, falls as rain. Breath is in everything. Now the claim. You'll hear in wellness writing that prana is basically oxygen, or that it's a hidden energy a machine can read. The first is too small: the Prashna's breath is fire and rain and the life of creatures, not one gas in the lungs. The second is a different kind of claim altogether. The Upanishad never offers prana as something to measure. It offers a way of seeing a living thing as held together by something it doesn't control. So read prana as a teaching about life, not a reading on a dial. What a person can actually watch is the breath itself, going out and coming back. The Prashna asks for nothing more.
screen: `THE SENSES EACH CLAIM THE BODY` · `BEES FOLLOWING THEIR KING BEE` · `BREATH AS FIRE, SUN AND RAIN` · `A TEACHING, NOT A READING ON A DIAL`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath rise and settle without steering it. As it rises, notice what rises with it, the chest, the shoulders, maybe a thought; as it settles, let speech go quiet and the eyes rest, the swarm following its king bee. If you pray, you can offer one breath back with thanks.
The breath again. In the Prashna, breath gets up to leave and every other power rises with it, like bees with their king. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. In the Prashna, breath is the one that holds the body up. See you tomorrow.

1323.title: the breath again — every claim checked
1323.hook: a student asks one question too many about breath, and the teacher answers anyway, with a king and his officers
1323.carry: the breath again — every claim checked
1323.tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked
1323.howItsDone: Teachers of yoga and Ayurveda use the names prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana to describe movements of breath in the body, and some treat them as a way of paying attention rather than as anatomy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: the senses quarreled, and breath settled it by getting up to leave, all of them rising like bees.

Some questions go past the lesson plan. In the Prashna Upanishad, the third student asks one. His name is Kausalya, and he doesn't ask what breath is. He asks where it comes from, how it gets into the body, how it splits itself up, and how it leaves. The teacher's first reply, in paraphrase, is a raised eyebrow: you ask more than you should. Then he answers anyway, because the student is sincere. Today: the map he draws, and what that map is and isn't.
screen: `THE QUESTION PAST THE LESSON PLAN.` → `YOU ASK MORE THAN YOU SHOULD.` → `HE ANSWERS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Pippalada begins at the source. Breath, he says, is born from the self, the way a shadow falls from a person. It isn't the self; it's what the self casts. Then the picture this chapter is remembered for. Breath works like a king who sends officers out to govern villages: you take this one, you take that one. So breath assigns itself. One current, called apana, works low in the body, with elimination and birth. Breath proper, prana, lives in the eye and ear, the mouth and nose. Samana, in the middle, spreads what's eaten evenly, the way a fire is fed. Vyana moves through the body's channels. And udana rises, and at the end, the text says, carries a person on. Now the claim. Online, the five winds are sometimes described as organs, with locations you could point to on a scan. The Prashna never offers a dissection. It offers a king and his officers, a shadow and the one who casts it: pictures, chosen to teach. Ayurveda's classical texts use the same names to talk about movement in the body, and on this path that's read as a way of noticing: the push down, the spreading, the rise. It isn't a diagnosis, and nobody should treat it as one. And one more thing the text quietly models: a hard question is welcome. The teacher grumbles, then gives his best answer to a student who asked too much.
screen: `BREATH FALLS FROM THE SELF LIKE A SHADOW` · `A KING SENDS OFFICERS TO THE VILLAGES` · `A MAP OF MOVEMENT, NOT A SCAN` · `THE HARD QUESTION GETS ANSWERED`

segments.voice: Let the breath come on its own and, for a few breaths, notice anything settling downward, the weight of the body on the seat; then the spreading, warmth or ease moving out from the middle; then the small lift at the top of each breath in. You're not finding organs, only noticing movement, the way the old map invites. If you pray, you can let one breath be a quiet thanks.
The breath again. In the Prashna, breath falls from the self like a shadow and sends out officers, like a king. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Questions past the lesson plan are welcome here. Back tomorrow, same hill.
